title: Risk assessments for new, non-routine, unplanned or specified tasks
plain: Do officers and ratings know the risk assessment procedure, and are risk assessments made and reviewed as the procedure says?
why: Jobs with no written procedure, and high-risk jobs like enclosed space entry, injure people when nobody stops to think first.
checks: Company procedure: when to make a new risk assessment and when to review one
Two sample risk assessments from the last three months
Whether each one fits our ship, our equipment and the actual job
Whether it was approved at the level the procedure says
Questions to a senior officer and to a rating who took part
ready: Risk assessment procedure and the standard recording form
All risk assessments from the last three months
Approval signatures at the correct management level
Records showing the crew reviewed the assessment before starting work
Date of last assessment, if none in three months
traps: Generic library risk assessment not adjusted to our ship or equipment
Assessment not approved at the level the company procedure requires
Specified task (hot work, enclosed space, working aloft) done without reviewing the assessment
New or unplanned job done with no risk assessment at all
Rating cannot say what the risk assessment for his job said
Procedure does not say who completes, approves or reviews the assessment
say: Under our SMS, any new, non-routine or unplanned job gets a risk assessment before work starts. For jobs like enclosed space entry, working aloft or hot work outside the workshop, we review the existing assessment with the team first. We record it on the company form and it is approved at the level the procedure requires.

practice.q: When do you need a new risk assessment, and when do you only review one?
a: New: any new, non-routine or unplanned task with no procedure
Review: specified tasks such as enclosed space entry, hot work, working aloft or over the side
Both are done before work starts

practice.q: Who takes part and who approves it?
a: A team, not one person, with suitable training and experience
Approval at the level set in the company procedure
Crew doing the job review it before starting

practice.q: (To a rating) Were you told about the risk assessment for this job?
a: Say what the hazards were
Say what controls were agreed
Say that you reviewed it before starting

tip: Take a library risk assessment and edit it for the real job: name the actual equipment and the actual hazards before it goes for approval.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices 1.25

title: Safety Data Sheets
plain: Is a Safety Data Sheet on board for every cargo, bunker, chemical and paint, and do crew know how to use it?
why: Without the right data sheet, crew do not know the health hazards, PPE or first aid for what they are handling.
checks: SDS for the cargo and bunkers on board during the inspection
SDS kept at each store where chemicals and paints are kept
PPE, first aid and eyewash at those storage places
How containers are stowed, labelled and closed
Whether the officer knows what the SDS is for and what it says
ready: SDS for all cargoes and every grade of bunkers
SDS for hydraulic oils, lube oils, paints, coatings, thinners and chemicals
SDS posted or kept close to where each product is stored
Company procedure for keeping SDS up to date
Cargo SDS in the format required by MSC.286(86) for Annex I cargo and fuel oil
traps: No SDS for the cargo or fuel oil on board
Annex I cargo or fuel oil SDS not in MSC.286(86) format
Benzene cargo SDS not meeting MSC.286(86)
Annex II or gas cargo SDS missing the safe carriage information
No local SDS at a chemical or paint store
No PPE, first aid or eyewash at the storage place
Unmarked, wrongly marked or unsuitable containers, or incompatible products stowed together
Officer does not know the purpose or content of the SDS
say: Our procedure requires an up to date SDS for every cargo, bunker, oil, paint and chemical we carry. They are kept at the point of use and the cargo and bunker SDS are in the cargo office. Everyone who handles a product knows to read the SDS for hazards, PPE and first aid before use.

practice.q: What does this SDS tell you about the hazards and first aid?
a: Show the hazard section and any toxic parts such as H2S or benzene
Show the PPE required
Show the first aid and spill action

practice.q: What do you do if a chemical comes on board with no SDS?
a: Isolate it and store it as the container says
Do not use it until proper information is available
Report it and get the SDS

practice.q: Where do you keep the SDS for paints and chemicals?
a: At or near the storage place
Printed on container, or posted where users can see it

tip: Walk every store before the inspection and match each product on the shelf to an SDS in the folder. Anything with no sheet gets isolated.

title: Simultaneous Operations (SIMOPS) procedure
plain: Do the crew know the SIMOPS procedure, and did we plan for jobs happening at the same time with controls in place?
why: Two jobs together, such as repairs during cargo work, create risks that neither job shows alone.
checks: Company SIMOPS procedure and its definition
Decision matrix and matrix of permitted operations, if you use them
Work planning meeting records, risk assessments and SIMOPS plans
How an officer explains SIMOPS on this ship
How a rating is told about SIMOPS and what he must do
ready: SIMOPS procedure
Decision matrix and matrix of permitted operations, if part of the procedure
Daily work planning meeting records
SIMOPS risk assessments from the last three months
SIMOPS plans or interface documents and the Bridge Log Book
Date of last documented SIMOPS if none in three months
traps: No SIMOPS procedure
Officer does not know the procedure or the matrices
No record that SIMOPS was considered in work planning
Controls not recorded in meeting notes, risk assessments or plans
SIMOPS happening without the required review and records
A SIMOPS the procedure specifically prohibits was taking place
Rating does not know the term SIMOPS or his own duty during it
say: SIMOPS means activities happening at the same time or place that can affect each other's safety. We raise them in the daily work planning meeting, risk assess the combined job, and use our matrix to see if it is allowed, restricted or not permitted. Toolbox talks make sure everyone knows the controls.

practice.q: What is SIMOPS and can you give an example on this ship?
a: Activities at the same time or in the same area that affect each other
Example: maintenance or bunkering during cargo operations
Avoid it where practicable, manage it where not

practice.q: How do you decide if two jobs can go together?
a: Use the decision matrix and the matrix of permitted operations
Risk assess the combined job
Approval at the level the procedure states

practice.q: (To a rating) What do you do when SIMOPS are ongoing?
a: Stay focused on your own task
Follow the controls from the toolbox talk
Stop and report if something changes

tip: Write SIMOPS in the daily work plan every time, even when you decide the jobs can go ahead. That entry is your proof.

title: Safety inspection of the main deck and mooring areas
plain: Do officers know the main deck safety inspection procedure, and do the inspections really find hazards?
why: The main deck is where slips, leaks, poor lighting and damaged mooring gear cause injuries and spills.
checks: Procedure for deck safety inspections by the designated Safety Officer
Inspection records and checklists
Deck lights tested, even in daylight
Walk of the main deck and mooring areas for anything inspections should have caught
Officer's knowledge of the checklist items
ready: Company procedure and the main deck checklist
Completed inspection records at the set intervals
Working deck lighting at all areas
Marked non-skid areas and trip hazards
Mooring fittings marked with SWL in tonnes
Drums and stores lashed on pallets, away from deck fittings
traps: No checklist, or records missing or incomplete
No non-skid coating on walkways and working areas, or areas not marked
Trip hazards not marked with contrasting paint
Cracked or broken light fittings, gaps in flameproof enclosures, paint over relief holes
Leaks from cargo, heating, inert gas or hydraulic systems
Deck lights out or lighting too poor for mooring or spill watch
Fairleads and rollers seized, or grooved and rough with synthetic lines
SWL not marked in tonnes by weld bead outline
Flammable liquids in a deck house not designed for it, or loose drums on deck
say: The Safety Officer inspects the main deck and mooring areas at the intervals in our procedure, using the company checklist. We record and close out each finding. Today you will see lights working, walkways marked and mooring gear free to turn, because we check these on every round.

practice.q: What do you check on the main deck during your safety inspection?
a: Non-skid, markings and trip hazards
Leaks, lighting and electrical fittings
Mooring fittings, fairleads and SWL markings
Weathertight doors and stowage of drums and stores

practice.q: What do you do with a finding?
a: Record it on the checklist
Fix it or raise the job
Follow up until closed

practice.q: Why must deck lighting be tested?
a: Safe access and mooring work
Spotting spills and leaks
Watching for unauthorised access

tip: Do one walk at night with the deck lights on. You will find dark spots and broken fittings that daylight hides.

title: Safety inspection of the machinery space
plain: Do officers know the machinery space safety inspection procedure, and do inspections find hazards before the inspector does?
why: Oil leaks, hot surfaces, loose plates and tied-open fire doors are the main fire and injury risks in an engine room.
checks: Procedure for machinery space safety inspections and the checklist
Inspection records
Walk through purifier room, workshops, steering gear, boiler room and stores
Lagging, guards, leaks, bilges, floor plates and fire doors
Officer explaining a few checklist items
ready: Company procedure, machinery space checklist and completed records
Covered metal bins for rags, emptied often
Lagging in place and free of oil
Guards on all rotating machinery
Clean light-coloured tank tops and bilges
Fire doors free of tiebacks, wedges or hooks, especially to the steering gear
traps: Checklist or records missing or incomplete
Paint, solvents, oil or wood stored in machinery space or steering gear room
Lagging missing, damaged or soaked in oil
Oil leaks, waste oil in bilges or save-alls, rubbish in bilges
Floor plates removed with open holes, or loose and uneven
Guards missing, spare gear or tools left near switchboards, batteries or steering rams
Gauge glass closing devices inhibited, or sounding caps missing
Fire doors held open with wedges or hooks
Broken lights, missing signs, pipelines not colour coded or labelled
say: The designated Safety Officer inspects the machinery spaces at the interval in our procedure, using the company checklist. We look at leaks, lagging, guards, bilges, floor plates and fire doors, and we record and close each finding. I can show you any item on the checklist.

practice.q: Why must fire doors to the steering gear room not be tied open?
a: They are self-closing fire protection
Machinery space fires are a high risk
Wedges, hooks and tiebacks are not approved

practice.q: What do you look for on hot surfaces?
a: Lagging in place and in good condition
Free from oil
Particularly near oil systems

practice.q: What would you check around the bilges and tank tops?
a: No waste oil built up
Painted light colour to show leaks
No rubbish blocking the mud boxes

tip: Do your own walk-round the day before, starting at the steering gear and ending in the purifier room. Check fire doors, floor plates and gauge glasses first.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices 5.5 and 20

title: Safety inspections of the cargo pumproom
plain: Do officers know the pumproom safety inspection procedure, and do the inspections catch hazards in the pumproom?
why: A pumproom can hold flammable gas, so a leak, a bad light or a failing fan can lead to fire or explosion.
checks: Procedure for pumproom safety inspections and the checklist
Inspection records
Pumproom walk: lights, ventilation, bilges, leaks, guards, rescue harness
Entry procedures posted at the entrance
Officer explaining checklist items
ready: Company procedure, pumproom checklist and completed records
Entry procedure at the door that matches the SMS enclosed space entry procedure
Lights and flameproof fittings in good condition
Ventilation on extraction, interlocked with lights, lower suctions open
Clean dry bilges and no flammable stores
Rescue harness rigged ready, safety chains in place, emergency stops marked, telephone working
traps: Records or checklist missing, or officer unfamiliar with the checks
Lights not working, or cracked glass, missing bolts or gaskets on flameproof fittings
Ventilation not on extraction, not interlocked with lights, or wrong suctions open
Fans noisy or vibrating
Wet or dirty bilges, or cargo drained to the pumproom bilge
Leaks from pumps, lines or glands, or bandage repairs on pipes
Spray shields missing, bulkhead seals defective, shafts unguarded
Paint or flammables stored, loose items, oil-soaked lagging
Rescue harness not ready, safety chains missing, emergency stops unmarked, telephone defective
say: The Safety Officer inspects the pumproom at the interval in our procedure, using the company checklist, and records the result. Before entry we follow the enclosed space procedure in our SMS. I can show you ventilation, lighting, bilges, rescue gear and emergency stops.

practice.q: How should pumproom ventilation be working during cargo operations?
a: Mechanical extraction running
Interlocked with the pumproom lights
Lower suctions open

practice.q: Can you drain line contents to the pumproom bilge?
a: No, it is an unsafe practice
Volatile product should not go to the bilge

practice.q: What rescue arrangements must be ready at the pumproom?
a: Rescue harness and rope rigged for immediate use
Checked regularly
Escape routes marked and clear

tip: The entry procedure posted at the pumproom door must be in line with the SMS enclosed space entry procedure. Compare them before the inspection.

title: Cargo machinery rooms safety inspections
plain: Do officers know the safety inspection procedure for cargo compressor and motor rooms, and do inspections find hazards?
why: Cargo vapour can collect in compressor rooms, so ventilation, airlocks and seals must work or gas and fire become a risk.
checks: Procedure for cargo machinery room inspections and the checklist
Inspection records and airlock alarm and shutdown test records
Entry and ventilation notices at the entrance
Ventilation pressure, fans, gas sampling heads and airlock condition
Officer explaining checklist items
ready: Company procedure, checklist and completed records
Records of airlock audible and visual alarm and shutdown tests
Entry and ventilation requirements posted at the entrance
Gas sampling heads set for the cargo carried
Bulkhead seal lubricator reservoirs topped up (or nitrogen seal working on LNG)
Oxide cargoes: compressor piping blanked or isolated
traps: No entry or ventilation notice at the entrance
Compressor room not at negative pressure, motor room or airlock not at positive pressure
Noisy or vibrating fans, blocked inlet or outlet grilles
Gas leak in the compressor room
Gas sampling heads or ventilation points wrongly set for the cargo, officer unsure where they are
Airlock alarms not working, no test records, damaged door seals, doors held open
Damaged or modified electrical fittings, cracked flameproof enclosures
Bulkhead seal lube reservoir low, unguarded shafts, flammables or loose items in the room
Blocked drainage, or compressors not isolated on Ethylene or Propylene Oxide cargo
say: The Safety Officer inspects our cargo machinery rooms at the interval in the procedure using the company checklist. We test the airlock alarms and shutdowns and keep the records. Gas sampling heads are set for the cargo on board and I can show you where they are.

practice.q: What ventilation precautions apply before cargo operations?
a: Fans running at least 10 minutes before cargo operations
Continue throughout operations
Run also if a leak is suspected

practice.q: Why do airlock alarms and shutdowns get tested?
a: Loss of ventilation pressure can let vapour in
Shutdown stops machinery when pressure is lost
Records prove regular testing

practice.q: How are gas sampling heads set?
a: High or low according to cargo vapour density
Lighter or heavier than air
Officer must know their location and status

tip: Know where each gas sampling head is and which way the changeover is set for the cargo on board. An officer who cannot point to them is a negative observation.

title: Safety inspection of the forecastle spaces
plain: Do officers know the forecastle safety inspection procedure, and do the inspections catch problems in the forecastle?
why: Forecastle spaces are wet, remote and contain enclosed spaces like chain lockers, so hazards are easily missed.
checks: Procedure for forecastle inspections and the checklist
Inspection records
Weathertight doors, lighting, water, tidiness and stowage
Marking and closure of chain lockers and connected spaces
Starter panels and anchor wash lines for leaks
ready: Company procedure, forecastle checklist and completed records
Weathertight door that closes and secures properly
Good lighting, dry and tidy space
Stores secured, no flammable liquids
Clear access to bitter end, safety equipment and bilge wells and alarms
Chain locker and thruster room entrances marked as enclosed spaces with entry controls
traps: Checklist or records missing, officer unfamiliar with checks
Weathertight door damaged or not able to be secured
Dark, wet, dirty or untidy space
Loose stores or spare parts
Flammable liquids stored in a forecastle not designed for them
Access to bitter end, bilge wells or safety equipment blocked
Chain locker not marked as an enclosed space or door not closed
Thruster room or pumproom entry controls not marked
Starter panels exposed to leaks, or leakage from anchor wash sea water lines
say: The Safety Officer inspects the forecastle at the interval in our procedure, using the company checklist. We check the door, lighting, leaks, stowage and enclosed space marking. Chain lockers and thruster spaces are marked and kept closed.

practice.q: Which spaces near the forecastle are enclosed spaces?
a: Chain lockers
Thruster spaces and connected pumprooms
Marked, closed or otherwise secured against entry

practice.q: What can you not store in the forecastle?
a: Packaged petroleum or flammable liquids
Unless the space is designed and classified for it

practice.q: What do you check for leaks in the space?
a: Anchor wash sea water lines and flanges
Water reaching starter panels
Door seal condition

tip: Look at the deckhead under the anchor wash line. Wet marks or rust trails show a leak, and inspectors look for that first.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices 2.5

title: Safety inspections of the accommodation spaces
plain: Do officers know the accommodation safety inspection procedure, and do inspections find fire and safety hazards?
why: Accommodation fires start from overloaded sockets, lint in dryers and clutter, and the crew sleep there.
checks: Procedure for accommodation inspections and the checklist
Inspection records and records of refrigerated room alarm tests
Cabins, public spaces, laundry, galley, pantries, stores and hospital
Sockets, electrical equipment, smoking rules
Weathertight doors, windows and portholes
ready: Company procedure, accommodation checklist and completed records
Weekly test records for the cold room alarm (and inside release)
Clean laundry and dryer vents free of lint
Hospital free for immediate use, not used as cabin or store
No overloaded sockets or damaged electrical items
Weathertight doors, windows and portholes that secure properly
traps: Checklist or records missing
Dirty, untidy, dark or obstructed spaces
Overloaded sockets or poor electrical equipment
Smoking rules not followed
Piles of clothing or lint in laundry or dryer vents
Weathertight door, window or porthole not closing properly
Hospital used as a cabin or storeroom
Refrigerated room alarm not working or not tested regularly
say: The Safety Officer inspects the accommodation at the interval in our procedure, using the company checklist. We look at electrical items, laundry, galley, stores, hospital and the cold room alarm. The cold room alarm is tested regularly and recorded.

practice.q: What are common causes of fires in accommodation?
a: Faulty or overloaded electrics
Careless smoking
Galley oil fires, lint in dryers, damp stored linen

practice.q: How do you make sure someone is safe in the cold room?
a: Door opens from both sides and there is an alarm inside
Alarm and inside release tested at least weekly
Tell someone and take the padlock inside

practice.q: What should the ship's hospital be used for?
a: Ready for immediate use
Not an extra cabin or a store

tip: Keep dryer lint traps and vents clean and check them on safety rounds. Lint build-up is an easy finding to avoid.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices 2.2, 2.5 and 23.9

title: Ballast and/or bunker pumproom safety inspection
plain: Do officers know the ballast or bunker pumproom inspection procedure, and do inspections find hazards there?
why: Pumprooms are enclosed spaces with pumps, leaks and rotating shafts where hazards can injure or kill.
checks: Procedure for ballast or bunker pumproom inspections and the checklist
Inspection records
Walk-through: lights, ventilation, bilges, leaks, seals, guards, rescue harness
Entry procedure posted at the entrance
Officer explaining checklist items
ready: Company procedure, checklist and completed records
Entry procedure at the door that matches the SMS enclosed space entry procedure
Ventilation on extraction, lower suctions open if higher ones fitted
Clean dry bilges, no paint or flammables
Rescue harness rigged, safety chains connected, emergency stops marked
Plan for a single fan failure: temporary measures plus risk assessment and entry permit
traps: Checklist or records missing
Lights out or cracked, flameproof enclosures loose or missing bolts
Ventilation not on extraction, wrong suctions open, or single fan failed without temporary arrangements
Noisy or vibrating fans
Wet bilges, leaks from pumps, pipes, glands, or bandage repairs
Seals or grease and oil cups cracked, missing or low
Unguarded shafts, oil-soaked lagging, loose items, flammable stores
Rescue harness not ready, safety chains missing, emergency stops unmarked, telephone defective
say: The Safety Officer inspects our ballast and bunker pumprooms at the interval in the procedure using the company checklist. Entry follows our enclosed space procedure, and the posted entry notice matches it. I can show you ventilation, bilges, seals, rescue gear and emergency stops.

practice.q: What if the only extraction fan fails?
a: Do not enter without temporary arrangements
Do a risk assessment
Issue an enclosed space entry permit

practice.q: What is checked on the bulkhead seals?
a: Seals and penetrations in good order
Oil or grease cups intact and above minimum level

practice.q: What rescue equipment is needed?
a: Rescue harness and recovery means rigged for immediate use
Safety chains on open vertical ladders

tip: Compare the posted entry notice with the SMS enclosed space procedure before the inspection. A mismatch can also count against question 5.5.1.

title: Lifting and rigging equipment procedures, maintenance and inspection
plain: Do crew know the lifting and rigging procedure, and is every lifting item certified, inspected, marked and fit for use?
why: Overloaded or worn slings, hooks, wires and cranes drop loads and kill people.
checks: Company procedure for lifting and rigging
Class and flag certificates for cranes, davits and loose gear
Inventory of gear not covered by class
Selected items for ID number, SWL and inspection marking
Questions to a rating about markings and pre-use checks
ready: Company lifting and rigging procedure
Valid certificates and periodic inspection records for class-covered equipment
Manufacturer certificates for all fall and topping lift wires
Inventory with storage place, date in service, SWL, last inspection and proof load date
Unique ID, SWL and inspection status (e.g. colour code) on every item
Retirement criteria and records of gear removed from service
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it
Class certification not maintained, or class item defective or out of service
No inventory for non-class equipment, or inventory not kept up to date
No manufacturer certificate for rigging gear or crane wires
Equipment past retirement criteria or still in use when poor
Items missing ID, SWL or inspection marking
No competent person inspection at the defined interval
Rating does not understand markings or pre-use checks
Officer does not know the inventory
say: Our procedure covers class-certified equipment and everything else, such as slings, shackles and chain blocks. Every item has an ID, a marked SWL and an inspection indicator, and it is on our inventory. The supervisor checks each item before every use.

practice.q: What does the marking on this sling tell you?
a: Unique ID number
Safe working load
Whether the inspection is current, for example colour code

practice.q: What do you check before using lifting gear?
a: Look for damage, wear and corrosion
Confirm SWL and inspection status
Do not use if in doubt, and report it

practice.q: When is gear taken out of service?
a: Meets company retirement criteria
Suspected overload or damage
Needs examination before use again

tip: Walk the store with the inventory in your hand. Any item with a missing tag or no matching line should be sorted before the inspector arrives.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices ch 19

title: Spare parts for a single cargo hose handling crane
plain: With only one hose crane, do we have a risk assessment and spares to keep it working after one failure?
why: If the only hose crane fails, hoses cannot be safely connected or disconnected.
checks: Risk assessment for single hose crane operation
Spare hydraulic hoses against the crane manual list
Other spares the risk assessment identified
Spare parts inventory and the spares themselves
ready: Risk assessment for single hose crane failure
Inventory with hose length, diameter and end fittings
Crane manual list of all hydraulic hoses
At least one spare of each hose size and length, same specification and rating
Other spares named in the assessment (winch motor or kit, hydraulic pump or kit, wires)
traps: No risk assessment for the single crane
Missing spare hydraulic hose for one of the sizes or lengths
Spare hose not of the same specification or rating
Spares listed in the risk assessment not on board
Special purpose crane treated as a spare when it does not share the same parts
say: We have a single hose crane, so we risk assessed the failure of each key part. We carry at least one spare of every hydraulic hose size and length, and the other spares the assessment named. They are listed in the inventory and I can show you them.

practice.q: What is the risk assessment for?
a: Identify parts that could fail
Decide the minimum spares
Keep the crane working after one failure

practice.q: What spare hoses must you carry?
a: At least one for each size and length on the crane
Same specification and rating

tip: Check the crane manual hose list against the spares store label by label. Lengths and end fittings are what get missed.

title: Pilot boarding arrangements
plain: Do deck crew know how to rig the pilot ladder safely, and is it in good condition and rigged correctly?
why: People fall from badly rigged or damaged pilot ladders, and a fall can be fatal.
checks: Company procedure for rigging and recovery with supervision
Pilot ladder certificates, tags and maintenance records
Ladder condition against the ICS BPG checklist A4
Deck securing, handholds, gateway, lifebuoy, lighting
Questions to officer and deck rating, especially working over the side
ready: Company pilot boarding procedure and rigging drawings
Manufacturer certificates and in-service date for each ladder
Ladder tagged or marked so it links to its records
Manropes, lifebuoy with self-igniting light, heaving line, not connected to the lifebuoy
Working pilot boarding lights
Damaged or retired ladders clearly marked or removed
traps: No procedure, or officer or rating unfamiliar with it
Ladder with no ID, certificate or maintenance records
Shackles, splices or knots in side ropes, uneven or painted steps, loops or tripping lines
Repair not following the manufacturer's instructions
Ladder weight taken by a step instead of the side ropes
Gateway opens outwards, no hold-back, or blocks the pilot
No anti-slip deck, handholds or bulwark ladder missing
Boarding position outside the parallel body, or combination ladder securing broken
Boarding light defective, retired ladder not marked
say: A responsible officer supervises the rigging with a link to the bridge. We inspect the ladder before each use, rig to our drawing and BPG checklist A4, and check lighting, lifebuoy, heaving line and manropes. Everyone doing the work knows the precautions for working over the side.

practice.q: What would you check on the pilot ladder before use?
a: Side ropes continuous, steps level, equally spaced, clean and not painted
No cracks, damage or loose spreaders
ID tag and records match

practice.q: Who supervises, and how?
a: Responsible officer
With communication to the bridge
Escorts the pilot by a safe route

practice.q: (Deck rating) How do you work safely when rigging over the side?
a: Know the procedure for working over the side
Follow the supervision and precautions it sets
Report any defect before use

tip: Test the pilot light at dusk, not only in daylight. Lighting that looks fine at noon is often weak or aimed wrongly at night.

title: Accommodation ladders
plain: Do deck crew know how to rig the accommodation ladder safely, and is it in good order and used within its limits?
why: A damaged or wrongly rigged ladder can collapse or let someone fall into the water or onto the quay.
checks: Company procedure for rigging and recovery with supervision
Maintenance records, fall wire certificate and installation date, five-yearly load test certificate
Marking plates at both ends of the ladder
Condition of steps, stanchions, turntables, wires and lifting points
Lifebuoy, light and line, safety net and lighting
ready: Company accommodation ladder procedure and manufacturer's instructions or drawings
Maintenance record for each ladder
Fall wire manufacturer certificate and date of installation
Fall wires replaced within the previous five years
Five-yearly load test certificate
Lifebuoy with light, and line attached and marked per IMO Res A.1116(30)
traps: No procedure, or maintenance records missing or incomplete
Five-yearly load test certificate missing or overdue
Fall wires not renewed within five years, or no manufacturer certificate
Fall wire too short for maximum freeboard with enough turns on the drum
No marking plate showing angle limits and design load
Cracks, heavy corrosion, bent steps or stanchions, seized turntables or rollers, missing pins
Temporary repairs to structure or hoisting system
Lighting defective
Bottom platform not level, safety net not rigged when required, no lifebuoy, light and line
say: We rig the ladder under supervision using our procedure and the manufacturer's instructions. We inspect it before each use and keep the maintenance records, fall wire certificates and load test certificate. The lifebuoy, light and line are ready at the foot, and a safety net is rigged when our procedure says so.

practice.q: What limits are marked on the ladder plate?
a: Maximum and minimum angles of inclination
Design load
Maximum load on bottom end plate

practice.q: When do you rig a safety net?
a: As the company procedure says
Where a person could fall into the water or between ship and quay

practice.q: (Deck rating) How do you work safely when rigging over the side?
a: Follow the procedure and supervision
Say what precautions you use outside the ship's rail
Report defects before use

tip: Check the fall wire length against maximum freeboard and keep the certificate with the installation date beside the ladder records.

title: Safe access to the vessel while alongside a terminal/berth
plain: Do crew know the safe access procedure at the berth, and are the gangway, net, lifebuoy and warning signs right?
why: People fall between ship and jetty, or cannot escape, if access is poor, dark or badly rigged.
checks: Company procedure for safe access alongside
Gangway maintenance records, five-yearly load test certificate and marking plate
Gangway condition and lighting
How it is rigged: handrails, bulwark ladder, safety net, angle
Lifebuoy, light and line, and warning signs at the gangway
ready: Company safe access procedure
Manufacturer's instructions or drawings for the portable gangway
Maintenance records and five-yearly load test certificate
Marking plate with angle limits and design load
Safety net rigged where required
Lifebuoy, light and line at the landing area, plus ISGOTT warning signs and cargo specific signs
traps: No procedure, or gangway records missing or incomplete
Load test certificate missing or overdue
No marking plate, structural defects, worn treads, temporary repairs
Boarding area lighting defective
Used outside design limits
Safety net not rigged when required
Gangway resting on handrails not designed for it, no bulwark ladder
No lifebuoy, light and line, or line not attached
No warning signs, or none for H2S or nitrogen operations
Rating or officer unsure how to rig and recover it
say: Under our procedure we inspect the gangway before use, rig it within its design limits with a safety net where needed, and keep the lifebuoy, light and line at the head. At the gangway we display the ISGOTT warning notices and signs for any special hazard such as H2S or nitrogen operations.

practice.q: What notices are displayed at the gangway?
a: No naked lights, no smoking, no unauthorised persons
No mobile phones without the Master's permission
Specific cargo or process warnings such as high H2S or nitrogen

practice.q: When is a safety net needed?
a: Not needed on a shore gangway fixed with permanent handrails
Needed for other gangways, rope or chain handrails, or removable posts
Per company procedure

practice.q: What if the gangway rests on the ship's rail?
a: Rail must be designed to take the load
Provide a bulwark ladder to the deck

tip: Before the inspector arrives, walk from the cabin to the gangway as if it is night and fix any dark spot, missing sign or missing line on the lifebuoy.

title: Personnel transfer by crane
plain: Do officers know the procedure for transferring people by crane, and is the basket and its gear in good order?
why: A person lifted by crane can be dropped, struck or ditched if the basket, tag lines or plan are wrong.
checks: Company procedure aligned with the OCIMF transfer paper
PTB and accessory test certificates, crane certification for personnel use
Training records for designated personnel
Marking: SWL or capacity and empty weight
Pennant and two tag lines, plus risk assessment, plan and crane failure contingency
ready: Company personnel transfer by crane procedure
Manufacturer test certificates for PTB and accessories
Crane certificate for personnel transfer, if declared
Training records, and maintenance and inspection records for crane, PTB and accessories
Risk assessment and transfer plan for any transfer in the last three months
Two tag lines 16 to 19 mm, ends seized, and a crane hook pennant
traps: No company procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it, the PTB checks, the plan or the failure contingency
No test certificates for the PTB or lifting accessories
Crane not certified for personnel transfer despite what was declared
No contingency plan for crane failure
No training records
Maintenance or test records missing, or not following manufacturer or company rules
PTB or accessories not marked with SWL or empty weight
Tag lines wrong size, or knotted or back-spliced ends
PTB not retired per policy, or transfer done without a risk assessment or plan, or using something that is not an approved PTB
say: Our procedure follows the OCIMF paper: transfers are kept to a minimum, risk assessed, and have a written plan with a crane failure contingency. Before use we inspect the PTB, accessories, pennant and tag lines, and only trained personnel take part.

practice.q: Before a transfer, what do you do?
a: Consider whether the transfer is needed at all
Risk assessment and a transfer plan
Inspect PTB, accessories and crane shortly before

practice.q: What are the tag line requirements?
a: Two tag lines, 16 to 19 mm diameter
Ends seized, no knots or back-splices
Long enough to reach the water, never tied to a strong point

practice.q: What if the crane fails during a transfer?
a: Follow the contingency plan
Officer must know it in advance

tip: If you carry no PTB, be ready to speak well about the procedure instead: the inspector will focus on the plan, risk assessment and contingency.
refs: OCIMF Transfer of Personnel by Crane between Vessels 1st ed

title: Helicopter operations
plain: Do officers know the company helicopter/ship procedure, and was it followed?
why: Helicopter operations near a tanker bring fire, static, rotor and deck movement risks if not controlled.
checks: Company helicopter procedure and risk assessment, with last review
ICS Guide to Helicopter/Ship Operations on board
Completed ICS shipboard safety checklists
Training and emergency drill records
Emergency tools and equipment inventory, and Landing/Operating Area Plan
ready: Company procedure covering risk assessment, training, drills, area plan, checklist, roles, tools and cargo or crane restrictions
Helicopter operations risk assessment with review date
ICS Guide to Helicopter/Ship Operations (5th ed)
Completed shipboard safety checklists for past operations
Training and drill records
Emergency tools ready, stored out of the weather, and landing area plan
traps: Missing procedure or one of its required parts
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure or the ICS Guide
No risk assessment, or no review as the company requires
No record of training or emergency drills
No copy of the ICS Guide on board
No landing or operating area plan
Checklist not completed before the operation
Emergency tools not ready at hand
Cargo or crane restrictions not followed during the operation
say: Our procedure follows the ICS Guide. We have a helicopter risk assessment, a landing area plan, a Responsible Officer and deck party, and we complete the shipboard checklist before each operation. Cargo and crane operations are restricted while the helicopter is here, and we keep drill records.

practice.q: What does the Responsible Officer do?
a: Appointed by the Master
Checks the deck requirements before the helicopter arrives
Uses the shipboard safety checklist

practice.q: What emergency equipment must be ready?
a: Tools such as axe, crowbar, bolt cutters, fire blanket and first aid kit
Ready for immediate use and protected from the weather

practice.q: What hazards are in the risk assessment?
a: Weather and ship movement
Downdraught, rotating blades, noise
Static electricity, communication, crash on deck or ditching

tip: Keep a filled-in checklist from the last operation in the file as an example, and check the emergency tools against the list in the pre-arrival checks.
refs: ICS Guide to Helicopter/Ship Operations 5th ed
OCIMF Guidelines for Offshore Tanker Operations 7.4

title: Helicopter facilities
plain: On ships with helicopter facilities, do officers know the procedures and have the crew been trained?
why: A helideck on an offtake tanker brings fire, gas and crash risks that only trained and drilled crew can manage.
checks: Operations manual: risk assessment, roles, training, drills, checklist, tools, limits
Helicopter Landing Area Certificate or training records for HLO and HDA
Drill records and the ICS Guide on board
Completed shipboard safety checklists
Emergency tools and equipment
ready: Helicopter operations manual with routine and emergency guidance
Risk assessment and evidence of last review
HLAC, or HLO and HDA course records plus ship-specific familiarisation
Emergency drill records
Completed shipboard safety checklists
Emergency tools ready, and ICS Guide (5th ed) on board
traps: Procedure missing any listed element (roles, training, drills, checklist, tools, restrictions, limits)
Officer unfamiliar with the procedures or the ICS Guide
No risk assessment or review
No HLAC and training records incomplete for anyone involved
No emergency drill records
No ICS Guide on board
Checklist not completed before the operation
Emergency tools not ready
Cargo operation restrictions not followed
say: Our operations manual covers the risk assessment, roles, training, drills, the ICS checklist and emergency tools. Our crew hold HLO and HDA training or the ship has an HLAC, and we have done ship-specific familiarisation. Cargo operations are suspended during helicopter flights.

practice.q: What training do crew need?
a: Accredited courses such as Offshore HLO and Offshore HDA
Then ship-specific familiarisation
An HLAC can show suitable training

practice.q: What tanker-specific precautions apply?
a: Suspend cargo operations during flights
Keep inert gas pressure low, vents closed, monitor it
Abort if pressure rises towards the release valve setting

practice.q: What can stop helicopter movements?
a: Calm weather with vented hydrocarbon cloud
Helideck sheltered behind a high structure
Tanker may need to disconnect and move clear

tip: Keep the HLAC, course certificates and drill records in one folder labelled for helicopter operations, so you can show them in a minute.
refs: OCIMF Guidelines for Offshore Tanker Operations 7.4.2
ICS Guide to Helicopter/Ship Operations 5th ed

title: Escape routes
plain: Do crew know the escape routes from machinery spaces, pumprooms, accommodation and the ship in port, and are they clear and lit?
why: In an emergency people must get out fast, even in smoke or dark, and firefighters must get in.
checks: Company procedure for identifying and marking escape routes
Green escape signs along routes from all required spaces
Doors on the route: unlocked or quick release from inside, self-closing fire doors latch
Escape trunk lighting and no obstructions
Route from the accommodation to the shore access, marked and clear of tension moorings and manifolds
ready: Company escape route procedure
Green and white escape signs, plus photo luminescent notices in port
Escape routes free of stores and obstructions
Locked external doors with rapid release from inside, and a plan for firefighters to enter from outside
Working lights in escape trunks, every bulb
Marked route to the gangway, routed away from mooring lines under tension and manifolds in use
traps: No company procedure
Routes from accommodation, machinery, pumproom, compressor room or thruster room not marked
Officer cannot lead the inspector out of a place where a dead end is possible
External door locked or bolted with no rapid inside release
Nobody can show how to open the door from inside or how firefighters would get in
Escape route blocked or obstructed
Self-closing door that will not close and latch by itself
More than one bulb unlit in an escape trunk
Route to the shore access not marked, or runs over tight moorings or past the manifold in use
say: Our procedure requires every escape route from accommodation, machinery spaces, pumprooms and compressor rooms to be marked, clear and lit. External doors are not locked, or have a quick release inside, and I can show you the route from here to the gangway. We keep it clear of mooring lines and the manifold.

practice.q: Show me the way out from here.
a: Lead directly along the marked route
Know every alternative way out
Know where it leads to an outside deck

practice.q: If a door on the escape route is locked for security, how does it open?
a: From the inside quickly without key or tools
Firefighters can access from outside as the plan says

practice.q: How are escape routes marked?
a: Green signs with white words or symbols
Photo luminescent in port, with directional arrows

tip: Walk the shore escape route yourself in port, in daylight and at night. If you have to step over a hawser or pass the manifold, ask the Chief Officer to re-route it.

title: Cargo and bunker sample management
plain: Do officers know how to label, store, log and dispose of cargo and bunker samples, and are the samples kept safely?
why: Samples are flammable and sometimes toxic, and loose or old samples are a fire and exposure risk.
checks: Company procedure on sample marking, storage and records
Sample locker: location, ventilation, temperature, fire protection
Sample labels and logs, and ORB Part I or II or Cargo Record Book entries
Any samples stored outside the locker
Responsible officer's knowledge
ready: Company sample procedure with marking, storage and records
Sample logs with seal numbers, dates and final disposal
Locker not reachable from the accommodation and out of heat and sun
Fire detection and fixed firefighting nearby, or portable equipment
Cargo samples kept no longer than the procedure says (ISGOTT suggests three months unless told otherwise)
MARPOL bunker samples kept at least 12 months from delivery
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it
Locker too small, accessible from the accommodation or hot
Poor ventilation, no fire protection nearby
Annex II samples not stored inside the cargo area
Samples stored outside the locker, kept too long or not disposed of as required
Bunker samples not marked per MEPC.96(47) or MEPC.1/Circ.864/Rev.1, no log of samples
Annex I or II cargo samples not marked as required
Disposal not recorded in the ORB or Cargo Record Book
Reactive Annex II samples not separated, or inhibited samples kept past inhibitor life
say: Our procedure covers labelling, storage, logs and disposal. Samples are kept to the minimum in a locker not accessible from the accommodation, away from heat and with fire protection. Each sample is logged with seal number and date, and disposal is recorded in the correct record book.

practice.q: How long do you keep bunker samples?
a: At least 12 months from delivery under MARPOL
Sealed and logged
Disposal recorded in ORB Part I

practice.q: Where are samples stored?
a: Dedicated locker, not accessible from the accommodation
Ventilated, away from heat and sunlight
Fire protection fixed or portable nearby

practice.q: What do you do with inhibited chemical samples?
a: Check regularly for polymerisation
Keep only while the inhibitor remains active per certificate

tip: Clear old cargo samples at each opportunity. A locker with fewer, correctly labelled and logged bottles is easier to defend.
refs: ICS Tanker Safety Guide (Chemicals) 5th ed 6.7.12 and 6.7.14

title: Respiratory protective equipment
plain: Do crew know when to use breathing apparatus during cargo operations, and does the procedure ban filter masks for this?
why: Filter masks do not protect against cargo vapours or lack of oxygen, so using one gives false safety.
checks: Company procedure on respiratory protection in cargo operations
Whether it prohibits filter type respirators for cargo work
Any respirators seen in use during cargo operations
Officer's knowledge of the procedure
ready: Company procedure on respiratory protection that bans filter or canister masks in cargo operations
Breathing apparatus available and ready for cargo duties
Crew briefed on when breathing apparatus is required
Filter masks stored only for dust and debris tasks, such as chipping or grinding
traps: No procedure on respiratory protection during cargo operations
Procedure does not prohibit filter type respirators for cargo work
Officer not familiar with the procedure
Crew seen wearing filter masks during cargo operations
say: Our procedure says filter or canister masks must never be used in cargo operations because they do not protect against cargo vapours or lack of oxygen. Where respiratory protection is needed, we use breathing apparatus. Filter masks are only for dust, such as chipping or grinding.

practice.q: Can a cartridge mask be used when sampling or gauging?
a: No, not for cargo operations
Does not protect against hydrocarbon or toxic vapours or lack of oxygen
Use breathing apparatus

practice.q: When can a filter mask be used?
a: Only for dust and debris
Examples: chipping paint or grinding
Never in enclosed spaces

tip: Keep filter masks in the paint locker or workshop, not at the cargo control room or manifold, so nobody picks one up out of habit.

title: Decontamination showers and eyewash stations
plain: Do crew know where the deck decontamination showers and eyewash are, and are they marked, reachable and ready?
why: After a chemical splash, seconds count, and a frozen or scalding shower is no help.
checks: Company procedure that keeps showers and eyewash ready for use
Inspection and test records
Spot test of one station for frozen or scalding water
Marking and access
Rating interview on location and operation
ready: Procedure and planned maintenance entries for showers and eyewash
Records of inspection and testing
Clear marking and clear access at every station
Fresh water line insulated with heat tracing or a recirculation system
Heat tracing and insulation intact, not removed
Crew know where the showers are and how to operate them
traps: No procedure to keep them ready
Rating cannot say where they are or how to use them
Not ready for use, not marked or hard to reach
Not inspected and tested as procedure requires
No insulation, heat tracing or recirculation
Insulation or heat tracing removed from supply pipe
Water frozen in cold weather or scalding hot in strong sun
say: Our procedure requires regular inspection and testing of every deck shower and eyewash, which is in the planned maintenance system. They are marked, accessible and operable in all ambient conditions with heat tracing or recirculation. The crew know where they are and how to operate them.

practice.q: Show me how to use the eyewash.
a: Go to the nearest marked station
Operate it and flush eyes
Know it must work in any weather

practice.q: Why is heat tracing or recirculation needed?
a: To work in all ambient conditions
Prevents frozen supply in cold
Stops sun heated water scalding the user

tip: Check the stations as often as your procedure and maintenance plan require, and in very cold or very hot sunny weather confirm the water is not frozen or scalding.
refs: ICS Tanker Safety Guide (Chemicals) 5th ed 2.7.3 and 8.3.4

title: Cargo Record Book
plain: Do officers know how to keep the Cargo Record Book, and do the entries show every Annex II cargo operation correctly?
why: The CRB proves that noxious liquids were handled and washed in line with MARPOL, and port states check it closely.
checks: Company procedure for keeping the CRB, paper or electronic
Entries for a recent series of operations on one cargo, load to tank cleaning and washings disposal
Signatures of the officer in charge and Master's counter-signature on each page
Official cargo names per the Certificate of Fitness
Reception facility receipts, prewash endorsement and comparison with deck log
ready: Company CRB procedure with correction and late entry methods
Cargo Record Books for the last six months
Cargo records and Bridge Log Book for the same period
Receipts or certificates for tank washings to reception facilities
Port authority endorsement for prewashes
Electronic record book: flag or class Declaration, backup and recovery instructions
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it or the entries
Entries not accurate, missing operations, or not in order
Wrong cargo names, not the correct name per Certificate of Fitness
Entries not signed by the officer in charge, or pages not signed by the Master
No receipt or certificate for washings sent ashore
Prewash entry not endorsed by the port authority inspector
Washings discharged to sea against MARPOL Annex II
Annex I cargo operations written in the CRB instead of ORB Part II
Electronic book without Declaration, instructions or automatic offline backup
say: Our procedure says what operations to record, who enters them, when, and how errors and late entries are corrected. Each entry is signed by the officer in charge and every page by the Master. Cargo names follow the Certificate of Fitness and washings receipts are kept with the book.

practice.q: What must be entered in the CRB?
a: Loading, internal transfer and unloading
Prewash and tank cleaning, discharge of washings
Ballasting of cargo tanks and ballast discharge
Accidental or exceptional discharge

practice.q: How do you correct a wrong entry?
a: Follow the company correction procedure
Enter overlooked operations as the procedure says, keeping chronological order
Master verifies the entries and signs each page

practice.q: How long is the CRB kept?
a: Three years after the last entry
Kept on board, readily available for inspection

tip: Pick one cargo and trace it through the book from loading to final tank wash. If any step has no entry or does not match the deck log, correct it using the company procedure for errors and late entries.

title: Oil Record Book Part II
plain: Do officers know how to keep ORB Part II, and do the entries correctly show every Annex I cargo and ballast operation?
why: ORB Part II is the legal record of oil cargo, tank cleaning and slop discharge, and false or missing entries are serious.
checks: Company procedure for ORB Part II, paper or electronic
Entries for a recent series of operations on one cargo
Signatures of the officer in charge and Master's counter-signature on each page
Slop water discharge entries against the deck logbook
Reception facility receipts and matching ORB Part I entries for transfers from the machinery space
ready: Company ORB II procedure with correction and late entry methods
ORB Part II, cargo records and Bridge Log Book for the last six months
Receipts or certificates for wash water to reception facilities
Entries for oil discharge monitoring equipment out of service and back in service
Electronic book: flag or class Declaration, backup and recovery instructions
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it or the entries
Entries not accurate or incomplete, or recording a MARPOL violation
Not signed by the officer in charge, or page not signed by the Master
Corrections not following the company procedure
No receipt for wash water sent ashore
Slop water discharge to sea not complying with Annex I
Ballast loaded into a cargo tank after crude oil without crude oil washing
No entry for oil discharge monitoring equipment out of service
Annex II cargo operations written in ORB Part II instead of the CRB
Electronic book without Declaration, instructions or automatic offline backup
say: Our procedure sets out which operations we record, who enters them and when, how we correct errors and late entries, and Master signature of each page. Entries match the deck logbook and cargo records, and receipts for any washings ashore are kept with the book.

practice.q: What operations go into ORB Part II?
a: Loading, internal transfer and unloading of oil cargo
Ballasting and cleaning of cargo tanks, crude oil washing
Discharge of ballast and slop water
Closing valves after slop discharge, disposal of residues

practice.q: What if the oil discharge monitoring equipment fails?
a: Make an entry when it is taken out of service
And when it returns to service

practice.q: What links ORB II to ORB I?
a: Sludge or bilge transferred from machinery space to cargo slop tank
Needs matching entries in both books

tip: Compare each slop discharge entry with the deck logbook position and time. Mismatches are the quickest way to a negative observation.
refs: INTERTANKO ORB Part II guide 2nd ed

title: Oil Record Book Part I
plain: Do the Master and engineers know how to keep ORB Part I, and do entries correctly show all machinery space oil operations?
why: ORB Part I records sludge, bilge water and bunkering, and inspectors check the numbers against equipment capacity.
checks: Company procedure for ORB Part I, paper or electronic
About 10 uninterrupted days of entries against the sludge inventory, incinerator and 15 ppm capacity
Signatures of the officer in charge and Master's counter-signature on each page
Receipts for reception facility discharges, and ORB II entries for slop tank transfers
Bunkering entries against the BDN
ready: Company ORB I procedure with correction and late entry methods
ORB Part I and Engine Room Log Book for the last six months
IOPP certificate supplement (Form B) with tank capacities
Weekly sludge inventory
Receipts for sludge or bilge to reception facilities and Bunker Delivery Notes
Electronic book: flag or class Declaration, backup and recovery instructions
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it or the entries
Entries not accurate, incomplete or recording a MARPOL violation
Not signed by the officer in charge, or page not signed by the Master
Corrections not following the company procedure
No receipt for sludge or bilge discharged ashore
No reciprocal ORB II entry for transfers to a cargo slop tank
Sludge burnt or bilge discharged beyond the equipment's capacity
Disposals of sludge or bilge that cannot be accounted for
Oil residue tank capacities in the ORB not matching the IOPP supplement
Oil filtering equipment out of service without an entry, or bilge discharged in a Special Area without alarm and automatic stop
say: Our procedure sets out which machinery space operations we record, who enters them, when, and how errors are corrected. The Master signs each page. Our entries agree with the sludge inventory, equipment capacities, the IOPP supplement, receipts and bunker delivery notes.

practice.q: What machinery space operations go into ORB Part I?
a: Ballasting or cleaning of fuel tanks
Discharge of dirty ballast or cleaning water
Collection and disposal of sludge
Discharge or disposal of bilge water, and bunkering of fuel or lube oil in bulk

practice.q: How do you show that sludge disposal is consistent?
a: Entries agree with the weekly sludge inventory
Incinerator burning within its capacity
Receipt available for shore disposal

practice.q: What if the 15 ppm equipment is defective?
a: Record when it failed and when it returned to service
Inspector also records the defect under question 6.6.1

tip: Pick any 10 days and do the arithmetic: sludge in, sludge out, incinerator hours, 15 ppm run time. If the numbers do not add up, find out why first.
refs: INTERTANKO ORB Part I guide 4th ed

title: Garbage Record Book
plain: Do officers know how to keep the Garbage Record Book, and do entries and storage follow the rules?
why: Garbage dumped or recorded wrongly breaks MARPOL Annex V, and toxic items mixed into general waste are dangerous.
checks: Company procedure and the Garbage Management Plan
10 consecutive days of entries that include a port visit
Signatures of the officer in charge and Master's counter-signature on each page
Receipts for garbage landed ashore, by category
Garbage store and incinerator area, and a rating's answers on segregation
ready: Company procedure and Garbage Management Plan
Garbage Record Book and Bridge Log Book for the last six months
Receipts or certificates showing quantities by category for shore deliveries
Entries for food waste through a comminuter or grinder
Segregated, hygienic garbage store, with aerosols and batteries kept separate
Electronic book: flag or class Declaration, backup and recovery instructions
traps: No procedure or no Garbage Management Plan on board
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure, the plan or the entries
Entries inaccurate, out of order, unsigned, or pages not signed by the Master
No receipt for garbage landed ashore showing quantity and categories
Food waste through a grinder not recorded in the book
Overboard food waste not matching special area, distance from land or comminuted status
Garbage stored unhygienically or not segregated by category
Dangerous or toxic items such as aerosols or batteries mixed with general garbage
Rating cannot explain segregation, aerosols and batteries, or permitted sea disposal
Electronic book without Declaration, instructions or automatic offline backup
say: Our Garbage Management Plan and procedure say what we record, who enters it and how errors are corrected. Entries are signed by the officer in charge and the Master signs each page. We segregate garbage, keep aerosols and batteries separate, and keep receipts for shore deliveries.

practice.q: What is the Garbage Management Plan?
a: Written procedures for minimising, collecting, storing, processing and disposing of garbage
Names the person in charge
In the working language of the crew

practice.q: (To a rating) Where do aerosols and batteries go?
a: Collected separately
Not incinerated and not mixed with general waste

practice.q: What proves garbage was landed ashore?
a: A receipt or certificate with date, time, quantity and categories
Kept with the Garbage Record Book

tip: Check the book against the deck log for the last port call. Make sure the shore delivery receipt and the book entry agree on quantity and date.
refs: IMO Guidelines for the Implementation of MARPOL Annex V 2017

title: Ozone Depleting Substances Record Book
plain: Do the Master and engineers know how to keep the ODS Record Book, and are all ozone-depleting gas operations and leaks recorded?
why: Refrigerant gases harm the ozone layer, and every recharge, repair, leak and delivery must be traceable.
checks: Company procedure for the ODS Record Book, paper or electronic
List of ODS equipment in IAPP supplement section 2.1
Maintenance records of a selected item of listed equipment
Recharges, repairs, emissions, supply and shore discharge entries
Signatures and the Master's counter-signature on each page
ready: Company ODS Record Book procedure
ODS Record Book and equipment maintenance records for the last six months
IAPP Certificate supplement, section 2.1, listing all ODS equipment
Entries in kg for recharge, repair, leaks, supplies and discharge to shore
Receipt or certificate for ODS landed ashore
Electronic book: flag or class Declaration, backup and recovery instructions
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it
Equipment with ODS not listed in the IAPP supplement section 2.1
Entries not accurate, incomplete or recording a MARPOL violation
Recharge, repair, maintenance or leak not recorded
Not signed by the officer in charge, or page not signed by the Master
No receipt for ODS delivered to a shore reception facility
Corrections not following the company procedure
Electronic book without Declaration, instructions or automatic offline backup
say: Our procedure sets out which operations and emissions we enter, who enters them, and how errors are corrected. We record in kilograms every recharge, repair, leak, supply and landing ashore. Every entry is signed and each page is signed by the Master.

practice.q: What must be recorded?
a: Full or partial recharge
Repair or maintenance of ODS equipment
Deliberate and non-deliberate discharge to atmosphere
Discharge to shore and supply to ship

practice.q: In what units are entries made?
a: Mass in kilograms

practice.q: Where is the list of ODS equipment?
a: IAPP Certificate supplement, section 2.1

tip: Take one refrigeration unit from the IAPP list and trace its last service through maintenance records to the book. Any gap shows up quickly.

title: MARPOL Annex VI NOx compliance and record keeping
plain: Are the NOx documents and records for our diesel engines in order, and do the engineers know the NOx equipment?
why: Engines must meet NOx limits, and a Tier II engine run inside a NOx control area breaks the rules.
checks: Company procedure for NOx records
IAPP Certificate and a Technical File for each listed engine
Record Book of Engine Parameters where required
Tier and on/off records on entering and leaving a NECA, EGR record book, SCR monitoring records
Engineer knowledge of the NOx abatement system and the failure procedure
ready: Company procedure covering NOx records and electronic book instructions
IAPP Certificate listing engines in paragraph 2.2.1
Technical File for every engine on the IAPP
Record Book of Engine Parameters for engines needing Engine Parameter Checks
Records of engine Tier and on/off status for NECA entry and exit, if required
EGR record book for solid residues and bleed-off water, and SCR catalyst monitoring records
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it
Technical File missing for an engine on the IAPP certificate
Record Book of Engine Parameters missing or not kept per company procedure
No NECA Tier and on/off records on a vessel built after the applicable date
Tier II engine run in an applicable NECA
EGR residue and bleed-off water records not kept
Engineer unfamiliar with the NOx abatement system, the SCR monitoring strategy or the actions for a failure not fixed within one hour
No records of measured NOx levels for an SCR system
Electronic book without Declaration, instructions or automatic offline backup
say: We hold a Technical File for every engine on the IAPP certificate. We keep the Record Book of Engine Parameters, and record Tier and on/off status when entering and leaving a NECA. The engineers know the NOx abatement system and the action to take if it fails for more than an hour.

practice.q: How do you achieve Tier III?
a: Tier III is achieved with SCR or EGR equipment
Not run all the time, must be operating in a NECA
Engine design gives Tier I and Tier II

practice.q: What if the NOx abatement system fails and cannot be fixed within one hour?
a: Follow the company procedure for that failure
Engineers must know the actions in advance

practice.q: What records go with EGR?
a: EGR record book
Storage and disposal of solid residues and bleed-off water
Residues landed ashore, not discharged or incinerated

tip: Check the build date of the ship and which NECAs apply. Then check that your Tier records exist for every NECA transit since then.
